why: Parcel i leaves the warehouse at the end of day min(i, n-1-i)+1, so it is a job with a deadline that must be picked by then, and you may pick one parcel per day. That is deadline scheduling: sort by deadline, keep a min-heap of chosen weights, and drop the lightest whenever the heap holds more picks than the current deadline allows.
hints: Ignore the shipping story for a moment: by which day must parcel i be chosen before it is gone?
Parcel i has deadline d_i = min(i, n-1-i) + 1 and you get one pick per day. Maximise the total weight of picks such that at most d picks have deadline at most d.
Sort parcels by deadline; push each weight into a min-heap, and if the heap size exceeds the current deadline pop the smallest. The heap sum is the answer. O(n log n).
pitfalls: The pick happens before that day's shipping, so a parcel shipped on day d can still be picked on day d.
With odd n the middle parcel is alone on the last day; the number of days is ceil(n/2).
Simply taking the ceil(n/2) heaviest parcels fails when several heavy ones share an early deadline (both ends of the array).
statement:
The parcels stand in a row, parcelWeights[0..n-1]. Every day happens in this order:

  1. You choose any one parcel still in the warehouse that has not been chosen before, and add its weight to the efficiency.
  2. The first and the last parcel still in the row are shipped (on the final day of an odd-length row, the single remaining parcel is shipped).

This repeats until all parcels are shipped. Return the maximum total efficiency.

So parcel i is still available up to and including day min(i, n-1-i) + 1, and there are ceil(n/2) days, one pick per day.

Worked example: parcelWeights = [4, 4, 8, 5, 3, 2], so the last available days are [1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1].

  • Day 1: pick the first 4 (it ships today). Ship 4 and 2; row is [4, 8, 5, 3].
  • Day 2: pick 5. Ship 4 and 3; row is [8, 5].
  • Day 3: pick 8. Ship 8 and 5.
  • Total 4 + 5 + 8 = 17.
